1422.title: Sh-M
1422.hook: shem, a name, gives Exodus its Hebrew title, Shemot
1422.howItsDone: The Hebrew title of Exodus is Shemot, names, from its opening verse; some Jews speak of God as Hashem, the Name, and Jewish teaching prizes a shem tov, a good name, which Pirkei Avot sets above the crowns of Torah, priesthood and kingship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-S-A: nasa, to lift and to carry, the root behind Naso. Your line was lift. Today, a root of just two letters.

Roll call, first morning of school. The teacher reaches a name she has never seen, pauses, and takes a guess. The whole room turns to look at the kid whose name it is. Will they correct her, or let it slide all year? The second book of the Torah opens with a roll call of its own: "Now these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt; every man and his household came with Jacob." The book is about to tell how a family was put to hard labor under taskmasters. Before any of that, it says their names.
screen: `A TEACHER GUESSES AT A NAME.` → `EXODUS OPENS WITH A ROLL CALL.` → `NAMES BEFORE SLAVERY.`

segments.voice: Sh-M. Two letters, shin and mem. Shem: a name. The second book takes its Hebrew title from that opening verse: Shemot, names. English calls it Exodus, the way out; Hebrew calls it the names. First, the roll call. Genesis already listed these same sons going down to Egypt, so why again? The medieval commentator Rashi answers: to show how dear they are, the way God brings out the stars by number and calls each one by name. A midrash adds that the people were redeemed, in part, because they did not change their names. Second, a name for God that works by not being a name. You met the burning bush back in year one: Moses asks what name to give the people, and hears "I AM THAT I AM." Today some Jews, in everyday speech, call God simply Hashem: the Name. It's a way of speaking of God with care, without saying the holy name lightly. Third, a name you build. Ecclesiastes says, "A good name is better than precious ointment." The Hebrew is a pun: tov shem mi-shemen tov, a good shem over good shemen, oil. Perfume fades by evening. The name you earn stays in the room after you leave. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. To say someone's name properly is to tell them they're a person, not a number on a list. That's what the first verse of Shemot does for a family about to be worked as labor. Names matter.

Then let the names of people you love pass through your mind slowly, one at a time, the way the book of names begins. If you pray, you can hold each one before God as it comes.

1423.title: Numbers in letters
1423.hook: each letter has a number value; chai is eighteen
1423.howItsDone: Hebrew letters double as numbers, and gematria finds meaning in the sums; some Jewish families give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the value of chai, and Pirkei Avot calls gematria one of the after-courses of wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-M: shem, a name, and Shemot, the book of names. Your line was names matter. Today, the letters turn into numbers.

Three hundred and eighteen. That's the number Genesis gives when Abram hears his nephew Lot has been carried off by raiding kings: "he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen," and went after them. An oddly exact number for a rescue party. A reader could pass right over it. One rabbi in the Talmud didn't. He looked at three hundred and eighteen and saw a person. To see what he saw, you need one fact: Hebrew letters can also be read as numbers.
screen: `ABRAM'S RESCUE PARTY.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND EIGHTEEN.` → `ONE RABBI SAW A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Gematria. In Hebrew, each letter carries a number. Alef is one, bet is two, and so on up to yod, ten; then the tens, then the hundreds. So any word has a sum. First, one you may have seen on a necklace. Chai, alive, is two letters: chet, eight, and yod, ten. Together, eighteen. That's why eighteen carries a quiet meaning in Jewish life; some families give gifts in multiples of eighteen, wishing someone life along with the money. Second, back to Abram. The Talmud records a teacher who said those three hundred and eighteen men were really one man: Eliezer, Abram's servant. Add the letters of Eliezer, and they come to three hundred and eighteen. Read that way, Abram went to the rescue with one faithful helper, and the number was a name in disguise. Third, a sense of proportion. Pirkei Avot gives gematria its place. Rabbi Eliezer ben Chisma calls certain detailed laws the essentials, and calls gematria, along with the study of the heavens, the after-courses of wisdom. The side dishes: delicious, worth having, but not the meal. Even inside the tradition, the game has its place at the table. Fourth, an ordinary day. Gematria trains a reader to notice. A number that looks like filler might be worth a second look; a word might hold more than its first meaning. The letters aren't only sounds. Letters count.

segments.voice: If you know how your name, or a Hebrew name you love, is written in Hebrew letters, add up the values slowly, one letter at a time; if not, start with chai: chet is eight, yod is ten. Then let the sum go and sit with the word itself, and what it holds for you: a person, a memory, a hope. If you pray, you can give thanks for the life the word chai names.

1424.title: Everyday Hebrew
1424.hook: todah, b'ezrat Hashem, mazal tov, l'chaim
1424.howItsDone: Jews say mazal tov at good news, l'chaim over a raised glass, b'ezrat Hashem about plans for the future, and todah for thank you; some begin each morning with modeh ani, I give thanks, before anything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gematria: letters read as numbers, chai as eighteen, and Abram's three hundred and eighteen as one man, Eliezer. Your line was letters count. Today, Hebrew you could hear in any kitchen.

A grandmother hangs up the phone in her kitchen. Good news: the baby has arrived, a girl, and everyone is well. Within a minute the room has said four things. Mazal tov, from everyone at once. B'ezrat Hashem, from the grandmother, when someone asks when they'll get to visit. Someone finds a bottle, pours, and lifts a glass: l'chaim. And when the glass is handed across the table, a quiet todah. None of it is a prayer service. It's just a kitchen, with Hebrew doing a lot of work in it, and the smallest of the four carries a whole root inside.
screen: `A PHONE CALL: A BABY GIRL.` → `FOUR PHRASES IN A MINUTE.` → `THE SMALLEST ONE.`

segments.voice: Everyday Hebrew, one phrase at a time. First, mazal tov. People say it at a birth, a wedding, a new job, a finished exam. It works like congratulations; mazal is usually translated luck or fortune, and tov is good. Second, b'ezrat Hashem: with the help of the Name, the Hashem you met two days ago. Some Jews tuck it into talk about the future, when they'll visit, when the house will be finished, a small way of saying the plans aren't only theirs. Third, l'chaim, to life: the same chai you added up yesterday, eighteen. Fourth, todah, thank you. It's the plainest of the four, and its root runs back into Genesis: yod, dalet, heh, carrying thanks and acknowledgment. You met Leah's sons in year one. When she gives birth to yet another, she says, "Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah." In Hebrew, Yehudah, from the same root as todah. The psalm that repeats its refrain verse after verse opens with it too: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good." In Hebrew, hodu. And the short prayer some Jews say on waking, before anything else, begins modeh ani: I give thanks. Same root again. So the word for passing the salt shares its root with the name Leah gave a son, and with the first word of a morning prayer. Todah.

Then a second person, then something that isn't a person at all: the bed you slept in, the water in the tap, the breath you're taking now. If you pray, you can say modeh ani, I give thanks, the way some Jews begin each morning.

1425.title: A verse alone (Genesis 1:1)
1425.hook: read Bereshit bara Elohim in Hebrew, by yourself
1425.howItsDone: Genesis 1:1 opens the Torah and is read aloud in synagogue each year when the reading cycle begins again after Simchat Torah; some Jewish learners practice reading Hebrew on verses like this one, word by word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, everyday Hebrew: mazal tov, b'ezrat Hashem, l'chaim, and todah, from the root of Judah's name. Your line was todah. Today, one line of Hebrew, and you do the reading.

A single line of Hebrew, black letters, no English underneath. For a long stretch now, this path has handed you pieces: the shapes of letters, their sounds, the roots hiding inside words. Somebody else always did the reading. Today the roles switch. Here is the line the Torah scroll begins with: Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. In the King James words, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Today you take it apart yourself, word by word, and put it back together.
screen: `ONE LINE, NO ENGLISH.` → `THE ROLES SWITCH.` → `BERESHIT BARA ELOHIM.`

segments.voice: Go slowly. First, bereshit. The opening letter, bet, is a little word glued on the front: in. Then reshit, beginning. Some readers hear rosh inside it, the word for head, as in Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year. Second, bara, created. Its letters are bet, resh, alef. Now look back at bereshit: bet, resh, alef are its first three letters too. The verb is hiding inside the first word before you even reach it. Elohim follows: God. Third, a word English can't translate at all: et. It's spelled alef, tav, the first letter of the alphabet and the last. In Hebrew grammar it simply points ahead to the thing being acted on. But some readers have seen more in it: the whole alphabet, beginning to end, standing at the start of the world. Fourth, the pair at the end. Hashamayim, the heavens; ha is the. Ve'et ha'aretz, and the earth; ve is and, and there's et again, pointing at the earth too. Everything above, everything below. Now put it back together. Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. You've just read the Torah's opening line in the language it was written in, one word at a time. That's a verse alone: a line short enough to hold in one breath. Bereshit bara.

If you pray, you can let the verse itself be your words, the way it opens the Torah each year. Otherwise, let the last two words stay with you: the heavens, and the earth you're sitting on.

1426.title: Year four close
1426.hook: law, thought, streams, character, life and language
1426.tomorrow: Year five opens: the sources themselves
1426.howItsDone: Jews ask for understanding in the weekday Amidah, in the blessing that closes 'who graciously grants knowledge', and on finishing a tractate of Talmud some hold a siyum, a small celebration of learning completed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verse alone: bereshit bara Elohim, read by yourself, word by word. Your line was bereshit bara. Today is the last day of year four.

A man comes to Hillel with a dare: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. You may remember him from your first week. The Talmud says Shammai had already sent him away. Hillel doesn't. He gives him one sentence: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah, he says, and the rest is commentary. Then two more words, easy to skip past: go and learn. This whole year has been the go and learn: the long commentary that grew around that sentence, the way Jews argue, decide, pray, mourn, celebrate and speak.
screen: `TEACH ME ON ONE FOOT.` → `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` → `GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: The year opened with a promise: now, how it works. Here's how it went, in six words. First, law. The Mishnah and the Talmud, the oral Torah set down, rabbis disagreeing on the record, and the codes that turned argument into practice. The block closed with the Talmud called a sea: nobody crosses it, but everyone can swim. Second, thought. Maimonides, the physician and philosopher who argued that reason can serve faith. Then the hidden side: Kabbalah and the Hasidic masters, sparks scattered in the world and a light from creation kept hidden away. Third, streams. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, Renewal, secular and more, each described in its own terms and ranked against none. Many streams, one river. Fourth, character, life and language. Mussar taught that traits are built one ordinary day at a time. The life cycle walked from a baby's naming to a wedding canopy to a mourner's kaddish. And these last weeks, the roots: letters that turn out to be numbers, a break that holds a birth, a name that opens a book, and a single verse you read by yourself. Put them together and you get the year's line. Judaism isn't only something believed. It's a way of thinking, out loud and in pairs, and a way of living, at the table, the door and the graveside. That's why Hillel didn't stop at one sentence. Judaism thinks and lives.

segments.voice: Let the year pass in front of you: one argument from the Talmud that stuck, one teacher, one trait you worked on, one Hebrew root, just one of each if they come. The weekday Amidah, the standing prayer, has a blessing that asks God for knowledge, understanding and discernment, and closes by blessing God, who graciously grants knowledge; if you pray, you can say it now from a siddur, in Hebrew or in English. If you don't, sit with the plain wish behind it: to understand a little more next year than this one.
